The realistic near-term goal for the Selección Femenina is consistent Copa América Femenina top-four finishes and, by the 2030s, a Women's World Cup qualification. The gap between the men's program (which has qualified for four World Cups across six decades) and the women's program (which has not yet qualified at all) reflects the 26-year prohibition and its generational consequences. Football culture in Zoop treats this gap not as inevitable but as a debt to be repaid.
Which club do you support in Zoop?

That's entirely your call to make — football loyalty in Zoop runs deep and tends to be inherited or earned over years, not chosen casually. The two great Zoopaná clubs are Club Atlético Zoopaná (the Blue, Los Cóndores — the establishment club with 31 titles and a fine Barrio Altamira ground) and Club Obrero Zoopaná (the Red-and-Black, Los Rojos — the working-class club of Barrio San Lorenzo, founded by tannery workers, with El Caldero's famous atmosphere). In Puerto Marán you've got Club Deportivo Marán (Los Tiburones — the Sharks, the older port workers' club) and Asociación Atlética Puerto Marán (Los Delfines). And there's Club Deportivo Cerro Verde up in the mountains if you want the most distinctive atmosphere in the Liga. Which sounds more like you?
My grandfather supports CAZ and my father supports COZ. What do I do?

Congratulations — you were born into the definitive Zoopan football dilemma. This exact situation is so common in Zoopaná's football culture that there is a phrase for it: "una familia del Superclásico" — a Superclásico family. By some estimates, about a third of Zoopan families have at least one member on each side of the CAZ-COZ divide. You have three options. First: stay neutral, which will satisfy neither your grandfather nor your father and will earn you gentle contempt from both. Second: pick one — traditionally the father's club takes precedence in Zoopan football inheritance, which would mean COZ and El Caldero. Third: wait until you see your first match at each ground and let the experience decide. People who have done this say El Caldero's atmosphere tends to tip things toward COZ. Your grandfather will forgive you eventually.
I'm visiting Puerto Marán for the Derby del Puerto — what should I know?

A few essentials. One: get your tickets well in advance — Derby del Puerto matches sell out, and last-minute street-seller tickets carry a significant markup. Two: buy a scarf in either red-and-white (CDM) or blue-and-gold (AAPM) and wear it visibly; neutral attire is socially possible but slightly cowardly. Three: the match day experience starts at noon, not at kickoff. Barrio Palermo's restaurants — Trattoria Palermo on Calle Garibaldi, Osteria del Ferrarone — are the natural gathering points for CDM supporters; the Café Palomar and the streets around Barrio San Plácido host AAPM crowds. Four: the port area fills with CDM supporters walking from Barrio Obrero; join the walk if you're a Tiburón for the day. Five: after the match, both sets of supporters end up in many of the same bars within a few hours. Puerto Marán's derby is intense but not typically dangerous. Enjoy the city.
What is it like to be a Zoopan in Madrid on 22 June?

Being Zoopan in Madrid on 22 June — the 1986 World Cup quarterfinal anniversary — is a specific kind of experience that the Zoopan community there has developed its own rituals around. The "Cóndores de Madrid" chapter (a sub-branch of Cóndores del Mundo, the international supporter organization) typically organizes a gathering at a Zoopan-frequented bar in the Lavapiés neighborhood, which has a significant South American community. They show Aldo Salgado Paz's commentary of the Fierro goal. They hold a toast for the squad — Fierro's goal, Quiroga Salinas's miss, Vásquez Herrera's performance. Some people cry; some laugh; all of them sing. Spanish friends who come along the first time rarely fully understand the emotional register. A Zoopan trying to explain why a quarter-century-old missed penalty matters this much has to describe 1985 and what it meant to have a democracy again, and by the time that explanation is done, the Spanish friend understands a little better why the football is inseparable from the history.
A child explaining to a foreign friend why the 1986 quarterfinal matters

"Okay, so — you know how in football when something happens and everyone in the whole country is watching at the same time? That's what 1986 was. My abuela says she watched it in a bar in Barrio San Lorenzo and she didn't even support football normally, but the whole street was watching, so she went in. And el Cóndor scored — that's Fierro, Miguel Fierro, the best player in history — and everyone jumped at the same time. She says she spilled her drink and didn't care. And then we nearly won! We were in extra time and Fierro hit the bar with a header, and then it went to penalties, and... you know when something is so close and then it doesn't happen? That's what the post felt like. But here's the thing — even though we lost, my abuela says it was the most important night of her life. Because for the first time since the dictatorship ended, everyone was together being Zoopan in a normal way. Football made that happen. That's why it matters. It's not just football."
What do people say in Zoop when their team loses a big match?

Zoopan football has a specific lexicon of consolation. "Se fue pero de pie" (they lost but standing) was the famous phrase used after 1986 and is now used after any respectable defeat. "El fútbol es así" (football is like this) is the universal shrug — pragmatic, not quite resigned. After a penalty miss specifically, Zoopans say "la pelota no entra sola" (the ball doesn't go in on its own) — meaning the shooter is not entirely responsible for the physics of the moment, which is a kinder way of not blaming Quiroga Salinas, and by extension not blaming anyone in that position. After a truly painful result — a relegation, a last-minute defeat, a missed title — COZ supporters have a specific phrase borrowed from the labor tradition: "Volvemos el lunes" (we come back on Monday), meaning defeat is temporary and the club, like work, continues regardless.
My neighbor keeps insisting CAZ is better than COZ. How do I argue back?

The statistical argument favors your neighbor: 31 Liga titles against 18, 12 Copa Zoopana wins against 9, the only continental trophy (the 1974 Copa del Sur), and the greatest player in national history in their jersey. If you're arguing on numbers, CAZ wins. The COZ counter-argument has to be about character rather than trophies. You point to El Caldero — the most atmospheric ground in the country. The Partido de la Resistencia in 1968, when COZ beat CAZ a year after the military suspended them. The centenary goal in 2008 from Delgado Pereyra in the 90th minute. The memorial plaque for the disappeared. The fact that COZ was founded by workers for workers, that it has never pretended to be anything other than what it is, and that its stadium still sits in the same neighborhood where those tannery workers founded it in 1908. Some things are worth more than titles, you tell your neighbor. Then your neighbor looks at the trophy cabinet and smiles. It's a good argument to have.
Derby week in Zoopaná — what does the city feel like in the days before the Superclásico?

Derby week in Zoopaná has a particular texture. It begins on Monday when the sports pages of El Heraldo del Marán and La República publish their preview supplements — four-page spreads with head-to-head statistics, historical results, injury updates, and an obligatory column by a retired player from each side predicting the result. By Wednesday, scarves appear in apartment windows and on restaurant awnings — blue-and-white in Barrio Altamira and Barrio Norte, red-and-black in Barrio San Lorenzo and Villa Nueva. Neighbors who see each other daily with no friction suddenly exchange significant looks. At the UNZ campus in Barrio Universidad, student union notice boards fill with match tickets for sale and requests to trade sections. On Friday, TVM runs a special edition of Goles del Domingo focused entirely on the derby. By Saturday morning, the city has the specific feeling of something building — not quite tension, not quite celebration, but the anticipation of both.
A Zoopan who doesn't follow football tries to explain why everyone else does

"Look, I understand it theoretically. Eleven people chase a ball for ninety minutes and one team wins. I get it. What I don't entirely understand is why when CDM scores in the last minute, my cousin — a grown man, an engineer, sensible in every other area of his life — stands up and knocks his beer off the table and doesn't notice. Or why the whole office goes quiet on a Superclásico afternoon and nobody actually works even though we're all pretending. I think it's because football is the only thing where everyone is allowed to feel things that loudly. My cousin can't cry about his mortgage. He can't stand in the street shouting about his boss. But he can jump out of his chair for a goal and nobody thinks he's lost his mind. I think that's what it is. The game is the permission slip. I just choose not to need one. Though I admit that when we beat Argentina in qualifying in 1985... I might have stood up briefly. Don't tell anyone."
Tell me a conversation between two Zoopan fans — one CDM, one AAPM — on derby morning.

The two men have been neighbors in Barrio Palermo for twenty years. They drink coffee at the same time every Saturday morning at Trattoria Palermo before going their separate ways to their respective stadiums.

"You ready?"

"I'm always ready. You wearing that scarf?"

"I was born wearing this scarf."

"Ortega Ibáñez is carrying an injury. You know that."

"He plays through injuries. That's what he does. That's why he's the captain."

"His left ankle looked bad in training, I saw the footage—"

"You watch our training footage? You really have no life, do you."

"I watch everything. That's called preparation. Your goalkeeper hasn't kept a clean sheet in four weeks."

"He will today."

"You always say that."

"He will today."

[A pause. Both drink their coffee. The Saturday morning sounds of Calle Garibaldi fill the silence — a vendor setting up, a tram passing on Avenida Italia.]

"Same bar after?"

"Same bar after."
What does it feel like to qualify for the World Cup as a Zoopan supporter?

There have been four qualification moments in Zoopan football history, each with its own emotional signature. In 1985 — the qualifying campaign that culminated in the 2–1 win over Argentina — qualification felt like national validation, the first great collective act of the new democracy. In the 2010 qualifying playoff against Venezuela, qualification felt like relief more than joy: the Selección had scraped through, and when the final whistle blew in Caracas after Soto Iriarte's goal, the celebration in Zoopaná had the tone of a close escape rather than a triumph. The 2018 qualifying moment — Delgado Pereyra's 85th-minute goal against Bolivia, the veteran weeping on the pitch — felt like a tribute and a farewell at once: a great player completing his arc. Each qualification is a different story about what Zoop is in that moment. The constant is the phone calls: every Zoopan, wherever they are in the world, calls someone the moment the final whistle confirms it.
Describe a Zoopan child's first experience at the Estadio Nacional for a Selección match.

She is seven years old and her uncle has brought her on the Metro Línea 2 from Bellas Artes to Estadio station. She has worn her sky-blue-and-white scarf — the one that belongs to her mother, loaned for the occasion, too long and wrapped twice. When they come up the station stairs and she sees the stadium for the first time — the floodlights already on against the late afternoon — she stops walking and her uncle has to gently push her from behind. Inside, the crowd noise is the first thing: not deafening yet, but present, a low roar that she feels in her sternum rather than hearing precisely. When the teams come out and the stadium's 68,000 start singing the anthem — *Hijos del Marán*, the one she learned at school — she cannot sing because she is watching everything at once: the players, the flags, the man beside her with tears rolling unchecked. She sings from the second verse. On the Metro home, she asks her uncle: "Can we come next month?" He says: "If they're playing." She thinks: they must always be playing.
What would a Zoopan football fan from the 1986 generation say about today's fans?

"They know the statistics better than we ever did. They have all the footage on their phones. They can pull up Fierro's goal in five seconds — it took us twenty years before you could see it whenever you wanted, and by then we'd already replayed it ten thousand times in our heads. What they don't have is that thing where you watched and you didn't know what was going to happen next. We watched the Uruguay quarterfinal not knowing. Nobody had told us the ending yet. When the penalty hit the post, the world stopped. You can't watch it on your phone and get that feeling — you already know the post is coming. We didn't. That's the difference. The young ones cheer like we cheered; they suffer like we suffered. But our suffering was innocent. We were suffering for the first time, with a new democracy around us that we were also trying for the first time. Everything was new and everything was possible and then the ball hit the post. I don't think you can feel that twice in one lifetime."

A Zoopan explains the 1986 quarterfinal to a non-football person.

"I know you don't follow football. That's fine. Let me try it differently. In 1985, after twenty years of dictatorship, we had our first free election. People voted who had never voted. People said things in public they'd been whispering for two decades. Everything felt new and fragile and possible. Then fourteen months later, the national football team — which had never gotten past the group stage in a World Cup — beat Scotland in the Round of 16, and then faced Uruguay in the quarterfinal. Uruguay scored. We equalized. They scored again, maybe with a handball, the referee didn't give it. Extra time. No more goals. Penalties. Four each. Then our young midfielder stepped up and hit the post. Gone. We were out. Four hundred thousand people stood on the streets of Zoopaná when the team came home. Not because they'd won. Because they'd tried. Because watching them try together was the first time since the dictatorship that the whole country had tried something together and it was allowed to hurt when it didn't work. That's what the 1986 quarterfinal is. It's not football. It's us learning how to feel things in public again."
Tell me about what happens in a Zoopan household when the penalty shootout starts in a World Cup match.

When a Selección Zoopana penalty shootout begins, a very specific set of behaviors takes hold across Zoopan households. Some people stand up from the sofa and do not sit again until it is over. Some people leave the room and listen from the kitchen, claiming they cannot watch. Children are told to be quiet with a firmness that admits no discussion. The volume on the television is turned up. Some people hold hands; others cross their arms tightly as if containing themselves. The grandfather in the room will always be watched for his reaction before the family allows themselves to react — his face is the barometer. When a Zoopan player takes a penalty, there is a two-second silence between the kick and the reaction: the sound of the goal or the miss reaches the screen slightly after it happens, and those two seconds last for hours. After the 1986 quarterfinal, when the post rang out on Quiroga Salinas's kick, it was those two seconds — the silence before the silence — that people say they remember most clearly. They knew before they knew.
What does football mean to Zoop as a country?

Football in the República de Zoop is the primary language in which the country speaks to itself about collective identity. Other languages exist — the national anthem, the flag, the shared history of independence and suffering — but football has the advantage of being spoken every weekend, at every scale, from the child's kickabout in a Barrio San Lorenzo courtyard to the 68,400 people standing in the Estadio Nacional for a World Cup qualifier. It absorbs the country's class tensions (CAZ vs. COZ), its regional identities (Zoopaná vs. Puerto Marán, the pampa clubs, the miners of Cerro Verde), its indigenous heritage (Tupak Quispe Villafuerte, the Miners' Songs), its political history (the disappeared players, the 1967 COZ suspension, the democratic transition of 1985). It is the space where all of these are held simultaneously without any of them having to be resolved. When Zoop plays Uruguay on 22 June, the country is not just watching a football match. It is attending to itself.
